summary: Old Field Point Light, Long Island: lit 1824, granite tower of 1869, keepers Elizabeth Smith and Mary Foster, a steel tower from 1933, village-owned since 1935.

lens.where: Fourth-order Fresnel installed 1855 (LighthouseFriends) and moved to the 1869 tower; replaced by a DCB-10 aerobeacon in 1933 (Keeper's Log). The USLHS record gives a current optic, FA-251.

structures.note: Present tower on the granite dwelling. LighthouseFriends and the Keeper's Log say cast iron; the USLHS place record says wood. Height given as 28 ft (LighthouseFriends) and 46 ft to lantern (Keeper's Log).
Two-story granite keeper's dwelling with a square tower rising from its gable end (Board, 1894).
Octagonal stone tower, 30 ft from base to lantern; replaced in 1869 (Keeper's Log).
Five-room rough-stone keeper's house of 1824, used as the village hall since 1963 (LighthouseFriends).
74-foot skeleton tower carrying the light from 1933; removed in 1991 (Keeper's Log).
Brick oil house added in 1902 (LighthouseFriends); the village lists its oil shed on the National Register.

access.note: Grounds open; dwelling and tower closed (LighthouseFriends). The village invites visitors to get a passport stamp from its clerk-administrator (village site).

facts.agency: Village of Old Field (owner since the 1935 conveyance; the Coast Guard maintains the modern beacon)

events.note: Octagonal stone tower and five-room dwelling built by the Daboll brothers; final cost $3,999.25
Shoemaker first keeper, 1824; Board and Keeper's Log give 1824 for the light
Fourth-order Fresnel lens in the tower lantern
New tower and granite dwelling completed at $11,995.42, replacing the 1824 tower
Treasury letter of 28 January 1886 on a complaint against the keeper, Jayne, who was exonerated
Breakwater lights established at the Port Jefferson harbor entrance as adjuncts to the Old Field light
600 running feet of wire line fence and 150 running feet of garden picket fence built; various repairs
Keeper Ray rescued two men from a grounded powerboat and sheltered them for two days
Light removed from the lantern and shown from a new 74-foot skeleton tower
Light moved from the 1869 lantern to the skeleton tower; fourth-order lens replaced by a DCB-10 aerobeacon
Conveyed to the Village of Old Field for public-park purposes (Act of 28 May 1935; conveyance 9 August 1935)
Village told the Coast Guard would occupy the station as part of a wartime defense area; control returned after the war
Modern beacon back in the 1869 lantern; steel tower removed

keepers.name: Edward Shoemaker
keepers.note: USLHS gives 1823; the Keeper's Log says he began in 1824. He died on 21 December 1826.

keepers.name: Mrs. Shoemaker
keepers.note: Widow of Edward Shoemaker. The archive gives only 'Mrs. Shoemaker'; LighthouseFriends says her name is unknown. Replaced by Walter Smith on 5 June 1827 (Keeper's Log).

keepers.name: Elizabeth Smith
keepers.note: Widow of Walter Smith; kept the light more than 25 years, helped by her son Henry (Keeper's Log). Paid less than male keepers in 1855 (Keeper's Log).

keepers.name: Mary A. Foster
keepers.note: Said to be the daughter of Elizabeth Smith (Keeper's Log); kept the light until 21 June 1869.

keepers.name: George D. Lee
keepers.note: Civil War veteran, 102nd New York Volunteers (Keeper's Log). His father-in-law Azariah Davis kept a diary at the station.

keepers.name: Charles F. Jayne
keepers.note: Farmer reputed to be a violinist (Keeper's Log). Accused of neglect in an 1886 complaint; exonerated (Keeper's Log).

keepers.name: Edgar S. Maclay
keepers.note: Appointed 26 July 1895; left 1 September 1900; dismissed from the Navy Yard post in 1901 (Keeper's Log; LighthouseFriends).

keepers.name: Richard E. Ray
keepers.note: Previously keeper of the Stratford Shoal light (Keeper's Log). Last keeper at the station.

other_stations.name: Stratford Shoal Light
other_stations.note: Years not given; 'previously' in the Keeper's Log.

wrecks.outcome: Laden with sand, struck a rock a few feet east of the light and was filled with water by 8 p.m.; remains auctioned on 16 October for about $175 (Azariah Davis's diary, as quoted in the Keeper's Log).
Ran ashore near the light; captain Francis Weller complained of the keeper's neglect; Treasury letter of 28 January 1886; keeper Jayne exonerated.
Ran aground on the rocks in front of the station; keeper Ray rescued two men and sheltered them for two days.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The station was built in 1823 and first lit in 1824 (Keeper's Log; LighthouseFriends). The 1825 date in the directory and the 1824 date in the record are reconciled as 1824 with the 1823 construction.
LighthouseFriends and the Keeper's Log describe the 1869 tower as cast iron; the USLHS place record says wood. Not resolved; both are cited in the story.
The Keeper's Log gives $400 for 7.545 acres in January 1823; LighthouseFriends gives $600 for three acres. Both are cited in the story and left unreconciled.
LighthouseFriends and the Keeper's Log give the granite dwelling and tower as completed in 1869; the village's page says the lighthouse was built in 1868. The story states both; not reconciled.
The USLHS roster gives 1823 for Edward Shoemaker's service; the Keeper's Log says he began in 1824. The story gives the Log's 1824 and notes the roster's 1823.

notes_for_editor: Roster lines are matched by name and position: the USLHS place is 1.1 km from the station record (USLHS positions are only to the minute), so check the match. The Keeper's Log article (by Robert G. Muller and Stephen Fragano) runs in the USLHS magazine American Lighthouse, Summer 2008, pp. 3-7, under the Keeper's Log heading; the story cites it that way. It quotes the diary of Azariah Davis, which I did not read directly, so the diary entries are cited to the article. LighthouseFriends is copyrighted and used for facts and paraphrase only. The NRHP nomination (listed 2024) was not available: the NPGallery PDF returned a placeholder image. The village's 'Our History' page returned 404. The 1901 Board page is cited by scan page 97; the printed page was not confirmed. The 1896 Tribune article is unsigned. Do not confuse this station with Old Field Point, Maryland (Elk River post lights, Board 1899-1901). The Board's 1894 description gives 'established 1823'; the 1824 first-lit date comes from the archive and the Keeper's Log.
